articles.title: His Last Check-In Was 300 Yards Off the Trail

blocks.text: Jake goes hiking every weekend. He lives alone in the city while his parents and sister live back home, so everyone knows he's mostly offline on Saturdays and Sundays. His family only asks one thing: check in on ANLY once he's off the trail.
Out on the mountain, Jake likes to check in at every rest stop with location sharing turned on, letting his family follow his progress without having to text.

That Sunday, his last check-in came through at 2:40 PM—and then nothing. By 8:00 PM, there was still no "back at the trailhead" check-in. His sister texted with no reply; his mom's call went straight to voicemail. The family began debating whether to wait longer or call for help.
Then his sister opened ANLY and tapped his last check-in. The pin wasn't on the main trail—it was in a wooded ravine roughly 300 yards off course.

Without realizing it, Jake had followed a deer path off the main trail, so the "rest stop" where he checked in at 2:40 PM was already off route. By the time he realized he was lost, he had zero reception and a nearly dead battery.

His family called Search and Rescue and shared the exact GPS coordinates. Instead of combing the entire mountain, rescuers headed straight to that pin and found him within two hours—cold and exhausted, but uninjured.
One check-in and one location pin narrowed an entire mountain search down to a few hundred yards.

articles.title: Five Texts and Four Group Chats—Now Reduced to a Single Tap

blocks.text: Mia films travel documentaries in some of the most remote corners of the world. Just last year, she traveled through Kyrgyzstan, Mongolia, and the Faroe Islands.

Previously, every single landing meant the exact same routine: text her mom; message her ten-year-old son staying with his dad; check in on her editing team's group chat; reply to her best friend; and let her manager know she had landed and when the next video would drop. Five texts across four group chats on every trip—usually over spotty airport Wi-Fi.

Now everyone is on her Carer list. The moment her plane touches down in Bishkek, she taps check-in once. Her mom sees it, her son watches Mom's droplet turn blue, her editor knows footage is on the way, and her best friend sends back a heart.
"I used to spend my first hour in a new country answering the exact same question five times," Mia said. "Now I actually get to look around and take it all in."
Everyone who loves you wants to know you're safe—they shouldn't all have to ask one by one.

articles.title: Dad Said He Was Walking to Grab Breakfast—And Never Came Home

blocks.text: Mr. Baker, seventy-eight, lives alone in an older apartment in San Diego. Last year, doctors diagnosed him with mild dementia; he still manages day-to-day life independently, though he occasionally forgets things.

His older daughter works in Los Angeles, his younger daughter lives in Paris, and his son works in Austin. Busy with their own lives, the three siblings take turns calling every Sunday. They set up ANLY on their dad's phone, adding all three kids, Mrs. Carter across the hall, and his former coworker Mr. Evans as Carers. Every day right after lunch, Mr. Baker taps check-in.
That morning, Mr. Baker mentioned to Mrs. Carter that he was walking down to the corner bakery for breakfast.
By noon, he still hadn't returned. Lunchtime passed with no check-in.
By afternoon, all five Carers received an alert.

It was the middle of the night in Paris, so his younger daughter was asleep. His son was stuck in a meeting. His older daughter called twice with no answer and immediately phoned Mrs. Carter. Knocking on his door and finding nobody home, Mrs. Carter recalled their morning chat: "He said he was heading to the bakery, but that place closes at noon."

His older daughter called 911 right away to report him missing and shared a recent photo in the family chat. Seeing the alert, Mr. Evans drove slowly up and down the surrounding neighborhood streets looking for him.

By early evening, police officers found him near the neighborhood where he had lived thirty years earlier. Sitting on a park bench, he explained he was waiting for the bus—he just couldn't remember which route number to take.
That night, his older daughter drove down from Los Angeles. Looking a little embarrassed, her dad said, "I guess I just wandered a bit too far."

Afterward, the siblings and Mrs. Carter tucked an ID card with his address and emergency contacts inside his wallet, agreeing that whoever lived closest would check in person first if he ever missed a check-in again.
Five people received the alert, and three jumped into action right away—that was all it took.

articles.title: Do Your Parents Use Electric Blankets and Hand Warmers in Winter? Share These 5 Reminders

blocks.text: When temperatures drop, many parents pull out electric blankets, hand warmers, and hot water bottles. Used safely, they bring cozy warmth; used improperly, they can cause burns—especially for older adults whose skin is thinner and less sensitive to heat.

Preheat the electric blanket, then turn it off or set it to low before sleeping
Many electric blankets have auto-shutoff timers you can set up for your parents. Always check that cords aren't frayed and the blanket isn't folded tightly.

Never place adhesive heat packs directly on bare skin
Stick them over a layer of clothing, never wear them while sleeping, and avoid leaving them on the exact same spot for hours.

Don't fill hot water bottles with boiling water
Use warm rather than scalding water, wrap the bottle in a cloth cover, and take it out of bed before falling asleep.

Take extra care if a parent has diabetes or poor circulation
Reduced sensation in hands and feet means burns can happen without being felt right away. Ask their doctor or nurse for safe warming tips.

Use ANLY for a simple daily safety check
Winter brings higher household risks. Add yourself, your siblings, and nearby relatives as Carers for your parents on ANLY so they can tap check-in once a day. If they miss a check-in, every Carer will receive a reminder so someone can call and check on them first.
On cold nights, give home a quick call and remind them: "Don't forget to turn off the electric blanket!"

articles.title: The Very First App Grandpa Learned to Use

blocks.text: There are only two apps on Grandpa's phone that he knows how to use all by himself: WhatsApp, and now ANLY.

When his granddaughter first set it up for him, he grumbled, "It's not like I'm going to get lost." After two weeks, though, he started tapping the droplet at the same time every day—not out of fear of emergencies, but because he knew his daughter would see his smiling blue droplet appear.
"You get to see that I'm safe, and I get to see when you're busy or finally free to reply," he said. It has easily become the steadiest connection between father and daughter in over a decade.

articles.title: Her First Birthday Alone in a New City

blocks.text: This spring, Lauren moved from San Diego to Los Angeles for a new job. She barely knew her new coworkers yet, her college friends were scattered across the country, and her parents called once a week.

Her birthday happened to fall on a Monday. She worked her normal shift, stayed late for overtime, and didn't get back to her apartment until 9:00 PM. She tapped check-in on ANLY, thinking, "Well, I guess that's my birthday this year."
Ten minutes later, her buzzer rang. A delivery driver stood at the door holding a small birthday cake. The card read: "Saw your check-in—Happy Birthday! Love, your Carers."

Her college best friend Sophie had been waiting for her check-in all evening. Knowing Lauren would be working late, Sophie waited until her droplet turned blue—confirming she was safely home—before placing the delivery order. Lauren's mom and two other friends on her Carer list had pitched in together.
"I always thought check-ins were just for safety," Lauren said. "I never realized they could be the start of a surprise."
When you're alone in a new city, you don't need a crowd—just the few people who remember.

articles.title: The Night Before Finals, Her Check-In Didn't Show Up

blocks.text: Maya attends college in Austin and lives alone in a studio near campus. She has Type 1 diabetes and has known how to manage her condition since childhood. Her parents live in Houston and video-call once a week, trying not to hover.
Before starting school, she agreed to check in on ANLY every morning after waking up. She also added Chloe, a classmate living in the same building, as her Carer and explained her medical condition.
The night before finals, Maya stayed up late studying, ate very little dinner, and forgot to check her blood sugar before falling asleep. By 8:00 AM the next morning, she hadn't checked in.

Receiving the alert, Chloe texted and called with no response. Remembering what Maya had told her, she immediately asked the landlord to unlock the door. Maya was lying in bed, barely responsive. Chloe called 911 right away and told the paramedics about Maya's Type 1 diabetes.
Maya regained consciousness quickly and was taken to the hospital for observation. A few days later, she returned to campus to arrange make-up exams.
"I'm good at taking care of myself," Maya said, "but there are times when I simply can't do it alone."
Living independently with a chronic condition calls for a quiet safety net.

articles.title: 17 Million People in Germany Live Alone—Including 1 in 3 Adults Over 65

blocks.text: 17 million

According to preliminary 2024 Microcensus figures released in July 2025 by Germany's Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), roughly 17 million people in Germany live alone—accounting for 20.6% of the entire population, or nearly one in five residents.
Twenty years earlier, in 2004, about 14 million people lived solo (17.1%), marking a 21.8% increase over two decades.
Single-person households are now the most common household type in Germany, representing roughly 42 out of every 100 households in 2024.
The share rises steeply with age: roughly one in three adults aged 65 and older lives alone (34.0%), and among those 85 and older, more than half live solo (56.0%).
Living alone is often a personal choice. But it also means there's no one around who notices you every day.

That's the quiet gap ANLY is built to fill. Tap check-in once a day with family, friends, and neighbors added as Carers. Everyone sees you're safe today—and if a check-in ever goes missing, every Carer will receive a reminder so at least one or two people can reach out.
Source: Germany's Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), 2024 Microcensus (preliminary), July 2025

articles.title: Sisters in Different Cities, Connected by a Single Droplet

blocks.text: Hannah works in Seattle, while her younger sister Chloe married and moved to Portland. Caught up in their own busy lives, they usually only call once or twice a month, trading sporadic texts in between.

Ever since downloading ANLY, they've shared an effortless new habit: tapping check-in before heading out each morning. Seeing the other's droplet turn blue simply says, "She's up and out the door—everything's normal." No forced small talk, no searching for topics—just quiet companionship.

One week, Chloe checked in unusually late two days in a row. Hannah casually texted, "Super busy lately?" and discovered Chloe was hitting a rough patch at work and feeling overwhelmed. That phone call lasted nearly an hour—the deepest conversation they'd had in months.
"Without that little droplet, I probably wouldn't have thought to ask," Hannah said. Sometimes it isn't a lack of care; we just don't know when to reach out.

articles.title: 5 Things to Remember When You're the One Caring for Family

blocks.text: Put your own doctor's appointments and rest days on the calendar—they matter just as much as your family's checkups.
Line up someone who can cover for you, even if it's just for one day a month.
Keep your siblings updated on how you're holding up, not just how Mom and Dad are doing.
Check in on ANLY every day yourself—don't just watch your parents' check-ins; let them see yours too.
When you feel stretched too thin, call a friend or a caregiver support helpline before you hit a breaking point.
Caregivers are often the last ones in the family to be checked on. You deserve someone making sure you're okay every day, too.

articles.title: The Two Weeks Dad Worked Offshore

blocks.text: Ryan works at an offshore wind farm, spending two weeks at a time living aboard a service vessel. Since divorcing his ex-wife, his ten-year-old daughter Lily stays with her grandmother.
With unstable offshore reception and long shifts, he rarely gets to have proper phone calls with his daughter. Lily used to constantly ask her grandma, "What is Dad doing today? Is he safe?"

Eventually, Ryan made a pact with her: every day after his shift, whenever there was a signal, he would check in on ANLY. Every morning when Lily woke up, the first thing she did was open her grandma's tablet to see if Dad's droplet had turned blue.
"Blue means Dad finished work safely today," Lily said.

Once, rough seas cut off signal on the vessel for an entire day. Ryan texted Grandma and Lily the day before: "Might not be able to check in tomorrow, don't worry." The following night, the moment they sailed back into coverage, checking in was the very first thing he did.
Ryan says he can't be by his daughter's side every day, but at least he can let her know every day that Dad is doing just fine.

articles.title: How Four College Roommates Stayed Close After Moving to Different Cities

blocks.text: After graduation, four former roommates moved to different cities for work. At first, they scheduled weekly video calls, but gradually their calendars stopped lining up and the group chat grew quiet.

One of them suggested adding each other as Carers on ANLY—not to keep tabs on each other, just to see everyone going about their day safely when checking in. Whenever someone's droplet stayed gray longer than usual, another would drop a casual "Everything good?" which often sparked far more natural conversations than scheduled catch-up calls ever did.
"I used to think friendship required hanging out all the time," one of them said. "Now I realize simply knowing the other person is doing okay is its own way of staying close."

articles.title: In an Old Riad in Marrakech, She Fell Down the Rooftop Stairs

blocks.text: Hannah is a freelance graphic designer who travels the world with just her laptop. This winter, she rented a traditional courtyard house in the old medina of Marrakech, Morocco, planning to stay for a month.

With a seven-hour time difference from her family—her parents in Austin and her younger brother in Houston—they usually video-called once a week at most. Before leaving, she added her parents, her brother, and two college best friends, Grace and Noah, as Carers. "Check-ins are free anyway, so adding a few extra people gives me peace of mind," she thought. Every morning, she checked in before brewing her coffee. She had also posted photos of the house and a screenshot of her booking in the family Room.

One evening, she climbed up to the rooftop terrace to stargaze. The old house's stairs were steep, narrow, and had no handrail. Heading back down, she missed a step and tumbled halfway down the flight.

Her ankle swelled immediately and her lower back slammed against the steps, leaving her unable to stand. Her phone sat on a lounge chair up on the roof, out of reach. Tucked deep down a quiet alley, nobody could hear her calls for help. She pulled a throw blanket around herself and lay at the foot of the stairs all night.
The next morning, she missed her check-in.
By noon, all five Carers received an alert. Her parents called repeatedly with no answer.

Remembering the booking screenshot in the Room, her brother immediately messaged the host through the rental platform, while Grace chimed in on the group chat: "I speak some French—let me call him directly."

Living nearby, the host arrived that afternoon with a spare key. Knocking at the front door, he heard Hannah shouting with all her strength inside, unlocked the door, and called a cab to take her to the hospital.
Doctors confirmed a severe ankle sprain and bruised lower back—nothing a few weeks of rest wouldn't heal.
"Five people got that alert, and my brother and Grace jumped right in," Hannah said later. "Having just one or two people notice is all it takes."
Now, she still taps check-in every morning before making her coffee.

articles.title: You Made It Safely Through Another Year of Ordinary Days

blocks.text: At the end of every year, social feeds fill up with big milestones: promotions, bucket-list trips, new apartments, and major achievements.
If you didn't have a year full of headline moments, that's completely okay.
Day after day, you still woke up, went to work, made dinner, and came home. Some days were exhausting, some felt dull, and on a few hard days you wondered how you'd push through—yet you did.
Those ordinary days add up to an entire year.

You stayed healthy, avoided major crises, and made it through—and that alone is worth celebrating. People who care about you are quietly waiting for your updates, breathing easier simply knowing you're safe.
So in these final days of the year, don't pressure yourself to write an impressive highlight reel.
Just tell yourself: "You did well—you made it through another year safely."
And that is more than enough.

articles.title: His Car Broke Down Right Where Cell Service Ended

blocks.text: Kevin goes solo camping several times a year. Living in Denver while his parents live in Colorado Springs, he knows his mom and dad don't expect constant updates—he simply checks in on ANLY with location sharing at every stop along the drive.

On a mountain pass in Colorado, his last check-in was at 4:30 PM from a scenic overlook. Twenty minutes later, after driving past the last bar of cell service, his engine overheated and died completely. He pulled onto the narrow shoulder with zero signal as darkness closed in.
He was supposed to check in from the campsite by 6:30 PM. By 8:00 PM, his mom had called twice with no luck.
She opened ANLY and tapped his last check-in—pinned at that scenic overlook on the mountain highway. She called the local police and gave them the road name and his last known spot.
Just after 10:00 PM, a patrol car found Kevin bundled up in a sleeping bag in the driver's seat, roughly a mile past the overlook.
"They didn't have to search the whole mountain," his mom said. "They only had to drive down one road."

articles.title: Lost in a Norwegian Pine Forest, He Waited Until Dawn Under a Giant Tree

blocks.text: David, a software engineer, was transferred by his company to Oslo, Norway, moving ahead on his own while his wife and two kids stayed back in Seattle.

With a nine-hour time difference, busy school and work schedules meant they video-called twice a week while juggling daily life apart. Before he left, his wife set up ANLY on his phone, adding herself, David's sister, his college best friend, and two Oslo coworkers—Ryan and Emily—as Carers. Every morning upon waking, checking in was the first thing David did.

During his first winter in Norway, he fell in love with cross-country skiing. That Saturday, after tapping check-in, he drove solo to a mountain trail, posting a photo of the trailhead map inside the family Room beforehand with a caption: "Skiing here today."

By afternoon, the sky darkened abruptly and heavy snow moved in. Taking a wrong turn at a fork, David fell on a steep descent and twisted his knee so badly he couldn't stand. There was zero cell reception in the woods, and the freezing cold quickly drained his phone battery.

Remembering his backcountry safety training, he stayed put instead of wandering, sheltering beneath a thick spruce tree. Putting on every extra layer from his backpack, he kept moving his hands and toes all night to stay awake.
Sunday morning, he missed his check-in.
By noon, all five Carers received an alert. It was the middle of the night in Seattle, so his wife hadn't seen it yet; his sister called with no answer.
Seeing the alert, Emily immediately opened the shared Room, spotted the trailhead map photo, and called the local police alongside Ryan to give Search and Rescue the exact trail name.
That afternoon, rescue teams located David near the trail. He suffered mild frostbite and a sprained knee ligament, needing a few weeks to recover.
When his wife woke up and saw the group chat, she cried for a long time. "I was fast asleep," she said later, "thank goodness someone else was awake."
Five people got the alert, and Emily and Ryan acted immediately. Having just one or two people notice is enough.

articles.title: Living Alone and Tackling High Cleaning Tasks? Follow These 5 Safety Rules

blocks.text: Whether it's spring cleaning or getting ready for the holidays, solo dwellers often end up wiping high windows, changing ceiling bulbs, cleaning AC filters, or pulling heavy bins off top closet shelves. Whenever you climb up high alone, take extra care.

Use a sturdy step ladder—never a chair
Swivel chairs, folding chairs, and stools tip easily. Invest in a solid household step ladder and make sure all four feet sit flat on the floor.

Tackle high chores during daylight when you're alert
Never climb a ladder right after an exhausting workday, when drowsy, or after having a drink. Good daylight helps you see clearly.

Keep your phone in your pocket, not on the table
If you ever take a tumble, having your phone within arm's reach can make all the difference.

Ask for help with anything too high or too heavy
For ceiling fixtures, range hoods, or bulky storage boxes, invite a friend over or hire a pro.

Tap check-in that day so your Carers know you're safe
Add family, friends, and coworkers as Carers on ANLY and check in daily. Once you check in, everyone knows you're okay today—and if you ever miss a check-in, they'll receive a reminder.
A spotless home feels great, but keeping yourself safe matters most.

articles.title: Living Alone Doesn't Mean Carrying Everything Alone

blocks.text: When you live alone long enough, it's easy to fall into a habit: handling everything by yourself, and feeling like talking about being sick or having a rough day is just "bothering people."
Yet loneliness and simply living solo are two very different things. Most of the time, it isn't that nobody cares—it's that there's no easy, low-key way to say, "I'm not doing great today."
A single daily check-in gives you that quiet space: without having to explain a thing, you let the people who care about you know you're still here today.

articles.title: His Parents Promised Not to Call Every Day—ANLY Made Keeping That Promise Easy

blocks.text: When Lucas left Philadelphia for college in Boston, his parents made him a promise: they wouldn't call every single day. They wanted to give him space, and he wanted his independence.
What they didn't expect was how hard that promise would be to keep. His mom constantly picked up her phone, stared at it, and put it back down.
So they made a new deal: Lucas would check in on ANLY once a day, at whatever time worked for him. No phone call required, no reporting where he'd been.

For the first few weeks, his mom checked the app more often than she cared to admit. Gradually, it became second nature. Seeing the droplet turn blue meant he was safe, freeing her to go about her day with peace of mind.
Lucas says it helped him just as much: "Even if I go a whole week without calling, I don't feel guilty because they know I'm alive and well."
They still call each other—just no longer out of anxiety, only when they actually have something to share.
Giving someone space and staying close aren't opposites. Sometimes, the right tool lets you do both.

articles.title: Her Last Check-In Was at a Farm in Australia

blocks.text: Claire went to Australia on a working holiday, picking strawberries on a farm in Queensland. The nearest town was a forty-minute drive away, and cell reception was patchy. Her family back in California and her best friend Jenna chatted with her once a week.
She promised her mom she would check in on ANLY every day after finishing work and keep location sharing on whenever she changed jobs.
That week, after checking in at the farm, she didn't appear again. The next evening, Jenna received an alert. Calls wouldn't go through, and her messages went unread.

Jenna opened Claire's last check-in and saw the pinned location at the farm. She looked up the farm's name and called. The farm owner explained that Claire had injured her leg with farm equipment the day before and was rushed to the town hospital, losing her phone in the commotion.
Jenna called the hospital, spoke with Claire, and updated her family back home. Her mother said that night was the first time she felt her daughter wasn't so far away after all.
When working alone abroad, your last check-in location is often the starting point for someone to find you.

articles.title: A Freezing Night in Seoul: The Balcony Door Locked Behind Her

blocks.text: Chloe is a remote software engineer who moved to Seoul this fall, renting a small twelfth-floor studio through spring.

Between the time difference and everyone's busy schedules, they mostly traded a few photos in the family group chat and video-called once or twice a month. Her parents lived in Houston and her sister in Dallas. Before leaving, Chloe added her parents, her sister, two college best friends, and Ji-Yeon—a friend she met through a language exchange in Seoul—as Carers. "Check-ins are free anyway, might as well add a few extra people," she thought, tapping check-in every morning right after waking up.

That night, carrying a basket of freshly washed laundry, she stepped out onto the small balcony to hang it up. A gust of wind blew the sliding glass door shut with a sharp click. The old latch jammed from the inside, refusing to budge no matter how hard she pulled.

Her phone was charging on the desk inside. She knocked on the wall shared with her neighbor, but nobody seemed home. Below, traffic roared along the street; she shouted until her voice gave out, yet no one looked up.
Temperatures plunged near freezing that night. Layering the damp clothes on one by one and flattening a cardboard box from the corner to sit on, she curled up and waited for sunrise.
The next morning, she missed her check-in.
By noon, all six Carers received an alert. Her parents called repeatedly with no answer. Her sister texted the family group chat: "Can anyone reach Chloe?"

Ji-Yeon lived just two subway stops away. Remembering Chloe's apartment building, she took the afternoon off and went straight to the building manager. Taking a master key upstairs, they unlocked the front door and immediately heard someone knocking on the balcony glass.
Chloe's hands and feet were numb from the cold, and her voice was hoarse. Doctors confirmed mild hypothermia—nothing a warm drink and rest wouldn't fix.
"Six people got that alert, and Ji-Yeon was the one who showed up," Chloe said later. "And having just one person show up is all it takes."
Now, whenever she steps onto the balcony to hang laundry, she props the sliding door open with a slipper first.

articles.title: Father and Son Who Hadn't Spoken in Three Years, Connected by a Single Droplet

blocks.text: Noah and his dad had a huge argument over his career three years ago and had barely spoken since. Even when he went home for the holidays, they only exchanged a brief nod.
Last year, his younger sister set up ANLY for the whole family, saying it was for their mom. Noah ended up as his dad's Carer too. Every morning at 6:00 AM sharp, his father checked in.

Noah never mentioned it, yet he looked every morning. Seeing his dad's droplet turn blue meant he was up and heading to the park for his morning walk. For three years, it was the only daily connection between them.
One day, he noticed his dad's check-in location was always that same neighborhood park. Suddenly, he remembered his father teaching him how to ride a bicycle there every morning when he was a kid.
The day before Father's Day, Noah sent a text: "I'll come meet you at the park tomorrow morning."
His father replied with a single word: "Okay."
Some words are hard to say out loud. Yet a daily check-in lets both sides know the other is still there—and the door is still open.

articles.title: The Morning After the Company Holiday Party, He Never Checked In

blocks.text: After graduating from college, Tyler moved to Chicago on his own for work, attending his very first company holiday party this year.

He was close with his family back in Denver, though none of them were big on phone calls—talking once or twice a month was plenty. When he moved to Chicago, his mom insisted he install ANLY. He added his parents, older brother, college roommate Jake, and two coworkers—Sam and Maya—as Carers, making it a habit to check in every morning before leaving for work.

At the holiday party that night, drinks kept coming around the table. Tyler rarely drank, yet ended up having several glasses. A coworker called him a cab home, and he made it up to his apartment on his own.
Stepping inside, he headed to the bathroom to wash his face. Suddenly dizzy, his foot slipped on the tile; his forehead struck the edge of the sink, and he collapsed onto the bathroom floor.
The next morning was Saturday—and he missed his check-in.
By noon, all six Carers received an alert. His mom called several times with no answer. His brother texted the group chat: "He had his holiday party last night—probably still sleeping it off?"
Sam got the alert too. Remembering how unsteady Tyler looked getting into the cab the night before, and living just a few blocks away, Sam replied to the group: "I'm heading over to check on him."

Arriving at Tyler's building, Sam asked the building manager to come upstairs with him. After minutes of loud knocking, a faint groan came from inside. The manager contacted the landlord, who hurried over with a spare key.

They found Tyler sitting on the bathroom floor with a large bump on his forehead, still dizzy. Sam took him straight to the emergency room, where a doctor put in a few stitches and advised rest, telling him to come back if he felt unwell.
That afternoon on the phone, his mom didn't scold him—she simply said, "Next time you have a few drinks, tap check-in the moment you get home."
Six people got the alert, and Sam was the one who knocked on the door. Having just one person show up is all it takes.

articles.title: Moving Abroad for Your Partner's Job? 5 Ways to Feel Less Isolated

blocks.text: While the relocated partner heads to an office every day with built-in coworkers and structure, the trailing spouse is often the one left home alone—navigating an unfamiliar language without local friends yet.

Build a steady weekly routine
Sign up for a local language class, join a fitness studio, or volunteer in the community. Having places to be gives your week rhythm.

Find local expat or hometown communities
Most major cities have expat spouse groups, international clubs, or online meetups. The first gathering can feel a little awkward, but showing up changes everything.

Share how you're feeling with your partner
Saying, "You're busy all day while I'm just waiting for you to come home," opens the door for both of you to figure things out together.

Don't rely solely on your partner to navigate local life
Save local emergency numbers, nearby clinics, and your building manager's contact on your own phone so you feel confident even when your partner travels for work.

Keep family back home reassured
Add your parents, siblings, close friends, and partner as Carers on ANLY and check in daily. Even on days when your partner is away on a business trip, several people know you're safe—and get alerted if you miss a check-in.
Moving abroad for love is a bold leap; your everyday well-being deserves care too.

articles.title: When Mom Calls Just to Ask, "Do You Have Enough Warm Clothes?"

blocks.text: Every year as soon as the weather turns chilly, Mom's opening line on the phone is almost always the same: "Do you have enough warm clothes?"
You tell her you're fine, and she sounds skeptical. You remind her you're a grown adult, and she replies, "Adults get cold too."
Eventually, you realize she isn't really asking about your closet.
She's asking whether you'd be cold out there on your own and not tell anyone; whether anyone would know if you got sick; whether anyone leaves a light on when you come home late.
Those thoughts feel too heavy to say out loud, so they come out as a simple "Do you have enough warm clothes?"
Next time she asks, don't just brush it off with "I'm good."
Snap a quick photo of yourself in your winter jacket. Tell her you had a hot bowl of soup today and plan to turn in early.
Let her see that you're taking good care of yourself.

articles.title: 5 Things to Do Before Traveling Abroad Alone

blocks.text: Save a screenshot of your hotel address—don't just save a link, in case you lose cell service.
Set your ANLY check-in frequency—while abroad, you can switch to checking in every 12 hours so family and friends stay updated on how you're doing.
Snap a photo of your passport and store it in the cloud, keeping your physical passport and backup copy separate.
Update your itinerary inside your ANLY Room so the people who care about you know where you're headed next.
Write down local emergency phone numbers and save them right on your phone's lock screen.
These steps take less than ten minutes, yet if an emergency strikes, those ten minutes determine how fast someone can find you.

articles.title: The First Year After Dad Passed, Mom Checked In Every Morning

blocks.text: Claire's father passed away last year. All three kids live in different cities: her older brother in London, Claire in New York, and her younger brother in Atlanta. Their mom insisted on staying alone in her longtime family home in Ohio, saying, "I'm used to it here."
The siblings agreed to take turns calling, averaging once every two weeks each, yet it never felt like enough. Their mom always answered, "I'm doing fine," leaving them unsure how to ask more.

Her younger brother suggested trying ANLY together. Hesitant at first, their mom soon realized a single tap let all three kids see she was okay—so she began checking in every morning after her grocery run.

Gradually, those check-ins became a quiet form of company. Before his meetings in London, her older brother saw Mom's blue droplet, felt at ease and walked into the meeting. When Claire noticed her mom checking in a little later several days in a row, she called just to chat about how she'd been sleeping.
"She didn't need us calling every single day," Claire said. "She just needed to know someone was thinking of her every day."
The days after losing a spouse feel long. One tiny daily gesture keeps faraway family woven into everyday life.

articles.title: A Note to Anyone Who Rarely Calls Home

blocks.text: It isn't that you don't love your family. You're just busy, or unsure what to talk about, or tired of having to give a full life recap every time you call.
So the calls gradually get fewer—once a month, then only when you happen to remember. Parents rarely complain; they just pick up their phone each day, glance at the screen, and set it back down.
If that sounds like you, try something far smaller than a phone call: check in once a day.
No small talk required, no topics needed. When your parents see your droplet turn blue, they know you're doing okay today—and you get to see theirs too.
When you eventually have something to share, you can still call. And when you do, that call will come from missing them—not from worry.

articles.title: She Thought It Was Just Food Poisoning—Until Her Friend Knocked on Saturday Afternoon

blocks.text: Last year, Rachel moved from Austin to Dallas for a new job, renting a studio apartment on her own. Her parents called every Sunday night, while everyone stayed busy during the week. Before moving, she set up ANLY and added her parents along with Jenna, a college friend living in Dallas, as Carers. Rachel made a habit of checking in every morning after waking up.

On Friday night, her stomach started aching. Assuming it was something bad from lunch, she took antacids and went to bed. She woke up several times in pain during the night, and by Saturday morning, she had developed a fever. She put her phone on silent, hoping to sleep it off, completely forgetting to check in.
Nobody was looking for her on a Saturday—not her office, and not her parents until Sunday evening. To everyone else, she was simply sleeping in.

That afternoon, her check-in still hadn't appeared, and her Carers received an alert. Jenna called twice with no answer, drove straight over, and asked the building manager to unlock the door. Rachel was curled up on her bed, unable to stand from sharp pain in her lower right abdomen.
Jenna took her straight to the emergency room. Doctors diagnosed acute appendicitis and operated that very day, telling her she was lucky she came in when she did.
"Without that alert, I might have tried to tough it out until Sunday," Rachel said.
When you first move to a new city, you don't know many people yet. Having just one Carer who lives nearby is enough.

articles.title: Dad's Check-In Appeared at a Park He Had Never Visited Before

blocks.text: Claire's dad was diagnosed with mild dementia last year. He still lives alone in Phoenix, takes his morning walk every day, and insists he's doing fine. Claire lives in Denver and calls him every Sunday.
They agreed on one simple routine: Dad checks in on ANLY with location sharing on after every morning walk. To him, it was just a quick way to tell his daughter, "I got my exercise in today."
For months, the pin appeared in the exact same spot: the neighborhood park two blocks from his house.
One Tuesday, instead of 8:00 AM, his check-in popped up at 11:00 AM—at a park across town, nearly three miles from home.

Claire called him right away. He sounded calm, just unsure which bus to take back. Keeping him on the line, she used another phone to call her cousin living nearby, who drove to the park and brought him home safely.
"He wasn't scared," Claire said. "I was the one who was terrified. Knowing his exact location made all the difference."
Soon after, they sat down with his doctor to plan extra support—a conversation that only happened because a single location pin showed them things were changing.

articles.title: When Should You Turn On Location Sharing? 5 Everyday Scenarios

blocks.text: ANLY only records your location at the exact moment you check in—and you can turn it off anytime. Here are five moments when turning it on makes sense:
Hiking or trail running: check in at the trailhead, the summit, and rest stops.
Solo road trips: check in when you head out, at rest areas, and once you arrive.
Arriving in an unfamiliar city or country: check in right after landing and when checking into your hotel.
Severe weather or natural disasters: if you evacuate or stay elsewhere, let everyone know where you're sheltering.
Heading home from a night shift: tap once when leaving work, and again when you walk through your front door.
When you're just at home or the office, leaving location off is completely fine. Whether and when to share is always up to you.

articles.title: Chasing the Northern Lights Solo? Do These 5 Things Before You Go

blocks.text: The Northern Lights usually appear in freezing, dark, remote places—often in the middle of the night. When chasing the aurora solo, getting home safely matters just as much as getting great photos.

Choose a setup where someone knows where you are
Whenever possible, join a local guided aurora tour or stay at a staffed hotel. If driving out on your own, leave your route and expected return time with the front desk.

Know winter road conditions
Roads near the Arctic Circle frequently ice over, and darkness falls early. If you aren't experienced driving on snow and ice, don't head out alone after midnight.

Dress one layer warmer than you think you need
Standing outside in sub-zero weather lasts for hours. Pack a thermal hat, insulated gloves, wool socks, and an extra down jacket—and keep a hand warmer near your phone so the battery doesn't freeze.

Carry a fully charged power bank
Extreme cold drains phone batteries rapidly. Keep a portable charger inside an inner pocket close to your body heat so your maps and phone stay alive.

Check in daily and post your itinerary in a Room
Add family and friends as Carers on ANLY and check in once a day so they know you're safe. Before heading out, post your hotel and aurora-chasing plans in a Room. If you ever miss a check-in, your Carers will receive a reminder.
The Northern Lights are unforgettable; making it home safely lets you share those photos with everyone.

articles.title: The Old TV in Grandma's Living Room Still Feels Like It's On

blocks.text: Growing up, winter break meant one thing you couldn't wait for: visiting Grandma's house.
In her living room sat a heavy old television playing afternoon reruns while she sat beside you, peeling fresh tangerines segment by segment.
Back then, time at Grandma's house seemed to move at its own gentle pace.

As an adult, visits grew fewer and farther between. One year, you came back to find that bulky old set finally replaced with a sleek flat-screen TV. Grandma said, "Your uncle bought it for me, and I still haven't quite figured out the remote."
You showed her how to change channels, and she nodded along—yet the next time you called, she claimed she had forgotten again.
The truth is, she didn't really forget. She just wanted you to show her one more time.
This winter, if you have a free weekend, go visit her.
Sit on the couch, watch an afternoon rerun together, and peel a tangerine for her.

articles.title: She Didn't Want to Worry Her Parents, So She Added Her Roommate as a Carer

blocks.text: Olivia is studying abroad in London. She texts her parents back in Boston about once a week—usually just a photo of dinner she cooked—because she knows they worry and doesn't want to give them any extra reason to stress.
Before she left, her mom asked her to set up ANLY. Olivia agreed on one condition: she also added her roommate Lily, knowing someone right next door would notice first if anything happened.
During finals week, Olivia came down with a fever. Telling herself it was just stress, she kept studying. By the second night, she could barely get out of bed and missed her check-in.

By the time her parents saw the missed check-in alert, it was 3:00 AM in Boston. Lily saw it over breakfast in London. Knocking on Olivia's door and hearing only a faint mumble, Lily walked right in and found Olivia burning up at over 104°F.
Lily rushed her to the hospital and texted Olivia's parents: "She's seeing a doctor right now, and I'm right here with her."
"I didn't want to worry my parents," Olivia said. "I never realized that staying silent was actually what scared them most."

articles.title: Her Last Check-In Was at a Beachfront Café

blocks.text: Yuki is a digital nomad spending six months in Bali, working from a local coworking space by day. Her parents back in California video-call once or twice a month. Alongside her parents, she added Tom—a friend she met at the coworking space—as a Carer.
She made a habit of checking in every evening after work and turning on location sharing whenever she was out.

That afternoon, she checked in at her favorite beachfront café, left her bag behind the counter, and went for a swim. The surf was rougher than usual, and a rip current pulled her out. A surf instructor managed to pull her back to shore, though she had swallowed a lot of water and was rushed to a nearby clinic—leaving her phone and bag back at the café.

That evening, she missed her check-in. Tom got the alert and called with no answer. Tapping her afternoon check-in, he saw the pin right at that beachfront café. He rode his scooter over, where staff told him her bag was still there and that a foreign woman had been taken to the local clinic earlier.
Tom tracked down the clinic, stayed with her until late that night, and texted her parents in California: "She's safe, and I'm right here with her."
"My parents are thousands of miles away," Yuki said, "but my last check-in told the closest person where to find me."
When living abroad alone, add a local friend as a Carer alongside your family.

articles.title: "Text Me When You Get Home" Is the Shortest Way to Say "I Love You"

blocks.text: Growing up, Mom always said, "Call me when you get there." As adults, it became, "Text me when you get home."
It's a short phrase, and an easy one to forget. Yet the person saying it is really saying: I'll keep thinking of you until I know you're safe.
When we live alone, travel solo, or live far from home, we often stay silent because we don't want anyone to worry. For the people who love us, though, silence is often harder to bear than bad news.
Checking in isn't about reporting your whereabouts or being monitored. It's simply placing that reassuring "I made it" right into someone's hands.
ANLY's daily check-in makes that timeless small gesture effortless: one tap, and the people who care about you know you're safe today.

articles.title: Los Angeles and Seoul: A Good Morning Seventeen Hours Apart

blocks.text: Nathan works in Los Angeles while his girlfriend Emma is in grad school in Seoul. With a seventeen-hour time difference, when she wakes up, he's about to finish work; when he wakes up, she's getting ready for bed.

At first, they video-called daily, but one of them was always yawning. Soon it dropped to every few days, often canceled because someone was too tired. It wasn't a lack of care—their schedules just never lined up.
Then they started using ANLY together. Emma checks in every morning when she wakes up, and so does Nathan. Nobody has to stay up late or set an alarm.

Nathan says his favorite moment is seeing Emma's droplet turn blue during his afternoon coffee break, knowing her day has started well. Emma says seeing his check-in before bed feels like hearing a warm "good morning."
Now they video-call every Saturday without needing to spend time confirming "Are you okay?"—they jump straight into sharing their week.
Distance can't erase time zones, but a daily check-in can still deliver "I'm doing fine today" right on time.

articles.title: His Coworker Noticed He Hadn't Checked In for Two Days

blocks.text: Leo is a freelance designer who lives alone in Seattle. He works from home, has an irregular schedule, and rarely reaches out to friends first. He added three Carers on ANLY: his college friend Matt, his older brother in Portland, and his former colleague Chris. Chris is also freelancing now, and they occasionally check in on each other's progress.

That Friday night, Leo had just told his friends he had a big project to rush and would "disappear for the weekend." But early Saturday morning, acute gastroenteritis hit him out of nowhere. He threw up until he had no strength left and collapsed in bed, unable to get up. His phone was in the living room, and he didn't even have the energy to walk over and grab it. He usually checked in before noon every day, but that day, nothing came through.

By the afternoon, all three Carers received an alert that Leo had missed his check-in. His brother texted, "Still alive?", but got no reply. Matt and Chris remembered he was on a deadline, assuming he had just muted his phone and was heads-down on his designs. No one thought much of it.

The next day, the alert came again. This time, Chris felt something was wrong: no matter how rushed the project was, Leo wouldn't go two whole days without checking in or reading messages. Chris called twice with no answer, let Matt and Leo's brother know, and drove straight over to Leo's place.
When he arrived, he found Leo so weak he could barely open the door himself. Chris rushed him to the ER, and after getting an IV, Leo slowly started to recover.

"If it weren't for that alert, everyone would've just figured I was still on deadline," Leo said later. After that incident, his Carers came to an unspoken agreement: whenever an alert comes, even if they think he's probably just busy, they call him first.

articles.title: "I'm Good" Is the Most Common Lie We Tell

blocks.text: When someone asks, "How have you been?" most of us automatically reply, "I'm good," no matter how we actually feel inside. It isn't about lying—it just feels exhausting to explain, and we don't want to be a burden.
Over time, "I'm good" becomes a polite reflex, burying real emotions even deeper. Eventually, the people around us stop asking twice.

A daily check-in doesn't require typing out a status update about your day. Yet it leaves an open door: on the days when you're truly struggling, someone who cares will notice an unchanged droplet and ask, "Hey, are you really okay?"—before you ever have to force yourself to speak up.

articles.title: Two Neighbors on the Same Floor Added Each Other as Carers

blocks.text: Mrs. Henderson and Mrs. Alvarez live on the exact same floor of their apartment building—both living alone, with adult children living out of state. Previously, they only exchanged polite nods in the elevator.

Last year, when Mrs. Henderson's daughter set up ANLY for her, she suggested, "It's smart to add someone who lives right nearby too." Thinking it over, Mrs. Henderson knocked on her neighbor's door. Hearing how simple it was, Mrs. Alvarez asked her grandson to install it on her phone as well.
From then on, both women saw each other's check-in every morning—no need to chat, just quiet reassurance that the other was up and about.

One morning at 10:00 AM, Mrs. Alvarez still hadn't checked in. Getting no reply to a text, Mrs. Henderson walked across the hall and rang the bell. Mrs. Alvarez opened the door with a raspy voice—she had been running a fever all night while her phone sat unheard in the living room. Mrs. Henderson checked her temperature, called her daughter in Texas, and brought over a warm pot of chicken soup.
"My daughter is states away and couldn't get here right away," Mrs. Alvarez said, "but my neighbor was just ten steps down the hall."
Often, the person who can help you fastest lives right next door.

articles.title: By 2050, Roughly 1 in 4 People in Germany Will Live Alone

blocks.text: 1 in 4
Household projections released in November 2026 by Germany's Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) point to a major demographic shift.
In 2024, Germany recorded roughly 41.8 million households, including about 17.9 million single-person households.
By 2050, Destatis projects total households could decline by 2% to 5%, while single-person households are expected to climb to between 18.5 million and 19.2 million.
Put simply, roughly 21% of residents lived alone in 2024—a figure projected to reach 23% to 24% by 2050, or nearly one in four people.
The fastest growth is occurring among adults over 60, especially those aged 80 and older.
As households shrink, fewer people are around to notice our daily routines.

That's why ANLY exists: a free daily check-in that lets family, friends, and neighbors know you're safe. You can add multiple Carers—and if you ever miss a check-in, everyone gets alerted so someone checks in on you.
Source: Germany's Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), household projections, November 2026

articles.title: About Half of U.S. Adults Are Experiencing Loneliness

blocks.text: 1 in 2

According to a 2023 advisory from the U.S. Surgeon General, about half of U.S. adults reported experiencing loneliness. The health impact of prolonged loneliness and isolation has even been compared to smoking up to 15 cigarettes a day.

Feeling lonely is not necessarily about whether you have people around you. Many people have families, friends, and coworkers, yet still feel like no one truly knows if they are doing okay today. Being left on read has become a daily routine, and "How are you?" has turned into a greeting no one expects a real answer to.

ANLY is not trying to keep everyone under constant surveillance. Instead, it offers a very light way for people who care about each other to maintain a simple connection—just enough to say, "I know you are okay today."
Source: U.S. Surgeon General Advisory, Our Epidemic of Loneliness and Isolation (2023)

articles.title: She Said She Was Going Camping for a Few Days—Until She Didn't Show Up for Work

blocks.text: This is based on a true news story.
In late September 2026, a woman in her seventies set out alone in her camper van for a multi-day camping trip in a Northern California forest. We'll call her "Mary."
According to her plan, she was supposed to return to work that Friday. When Friday arrived and Mary never showed up, she was officially reported missing.

The next day, two county sheriff's offices launched a joint search-and-rescue operation joined by volunteers and a California Highway Patrol helicopter. That same day, searchers located her camper van near a trailhead.
A day later, rescuers found Mary at the bottom of a steep embankment. Having fallen and spent days exposed to the elements, she had suffered several serious injuries and was airlifted to a hospital.
From departure to rescue, roughly six days had passed. The good news: she survived and was reunited with her family.
What makes this story so chilling is that silent gap—from the moment she left until she missed work, nobody realized anything was wrong.
Many people go camping or hiking solo not out of carelessness, but simply because nobody is expecting a daily sign from them.

If you often head outdoors alone, add family, friends, or even coworkers as Carers on ANLY. One daily check-in lets everyone know you're safe today—and if you ever miss one, they will receive a missed check-in alert instead of waiting until the day you're due back at work. You can also post your route inside a Room before heading out.
When just one or two people notice sooner, that dangerous silence becomes much shorter.
Names and identifying details have been changed to protect privacy.

articles.title: Moving Into a Coliving Space for the First Time? Check These 5 Things First

blocks.text: Many digital nomads love coliving spaces: you get a private bedroom, shared coworking areas, and a built-in community of fellow travelers. While lively and social, there are five things worth confirming before you unpack.

Read the lease and checkout terms carefully
Confirm minimum stay rules, security deposit refund timelines, and any early-departure fees in writing.

Ask who has keys or access codes to your room
Does your bedroom door lock from the inside? When does housekeeping or management enter? Where can you store valuables?

Get to know at least one trustworthy housemate
You don't have to be best friends with everyone, but knowing one or two neighbors means someone can knock on your door if you get sick.

Save building management and local emergency numbers
Is there overnight staff on site? Where is the nearest hospital? What are the local police and ambulance numbers?

Check in daily and save your new address in a Room
With people constantly coming and going in coliving houses, nobody might notice if you stay in your room all day unwell. Add family, friends, and even a new coliving buddy as Carers on ANLY, and tap check-in daily. When you move in, update where you're staying in a Room. If you ever miss a check-in, your Carers will receive a reminder.
Even in a bustling house, it pays to have someone who notices you're okay.

articles.title: In This Big City, She's the Only One Waiting for You to Come Home

blocks.text: When you first moved to this city, you didn't know a single soul.
Then, you adopted a cat.
Now, every evening when you unlock your front door, she hops down from the couch, pads slowly into the hallway, looks up at you, and lets out a soft "meow"—as if saying, "You're finally home."
On nights when you work late, riding the subway home, remembering she's waiting for dinner makes you walk just a little faster.
During those few days you were sick in bed, she curled up right beside your feet and never left your side all day.
People often say living alone is all about freedom. Yet having a little life waiting for you at home makes your days feel fuller.
Still, a quiet thought crosses your mind: what would happen to her if you ever didn't make it home one night?
So remember to let the people you care about know you're safe every day.
That way, both the cat waiting by your door and the people waiting for your updates can rest easy.

articles.title: She Didn't Make It Home from Her Evening Run Today

blocks.text: Sarah runs along the river trail every evening at 6:30. For nearly a year, rain or shine, she’s made it a habit to check in on ANLY right after she gets home and takes a shower. Her Carers include her good friend Emily who lives in the same neighborhood, her sister in San Diego, and her college roommate Jessica. They’re all used to seeing her check-in every night.

It got dark unusually early that day. As she reached the most isolated part of the trail, a dog suddenly darted out from the bushes. Startled, she lost her footing and tumbled down the grassy embankment. The moment her ankle hit the ground, the pain was so sharp she couldn't stand up. Her phone flew out of her armband and disappeared into the tall grass.

That section of the trail was usually empty, and it grew eerily quiet after dark. She tried shouting for help, but only the wind answered. Knowing she wouldn't be able to check in today, she hugged her knees, shivering as she waited.

Meanwhile, Sarah's Carers started receiving alerts that she had missed her check-in. Her sister called first, but no one answered. Jessica sent a text, which was left unread. Emily remembered Sarah's regular running route and decided to drive over to the trail to take a look, while the others kept trying to reach her.

Emily drove slowly along the road next to the trail, shining a flashlight down the embankment. Finally, she spotted Sarah huddled in the dark. She immediately called 911 for an ambulance and texted the others: "Found her. She's safe, but her ankle might be sprained."

Sarah often says now that the scariest part of that night wasn't the pain. It was the thought that if it weren't for that missed check-in, she probably would have been out there until the next morning before anyone noticed she was missing.

articles.title: My First Year Living Alone in a New City

blocks.text: At twenty-six, I moved out of my family's house and rented a small studio apartment in a city I had never lived in before.

In the beginning, everything felt new and exciting. There was the local diner where the owner quickly remembered my usual order, the riverside park just a ten-minute walk away, and a used-book market that only pops up on weekends. I signed up for a pottery class near my office and bonded with a classmate over several misshapen bowls. I even made a new friend at my favorite coffee shop after striking up a conversation about the book she was reading.

My days were full. I had places to go after work, plans for the weekend, and a fridge stocked with meals I was learning to cook for myself. I often thought about how wonderful living alone could actually be.

But occasionally, on certain very quiet nights, a thought would suddenly pop into my head: If I slipped in the bathroom, or if I woke up in the middle of the night with a high fever and couldn't get out of bed, who would notice? My new friends were great, but they wouldn't think to check on me every single day. My family loved me, but they were in another city and didn't know how my day-to-day life was going.

That was the first time I seriously opened ANLY. I added my parents, my sister, and my closest friend from pottery class as my Carers. It started as just a trial, a quick tap before going to sleep every night.

Over time, it slowly became a habit, as natural as brushing my teeth. That check-in isn't about reporting my whereabouts; it's just a way to let the people who care about me know that I'm doing fine today. And with that peace of mind, I could finally, little by little, turn this new city into my true home.

articles.title: Her Last Check-In Was in the Hospital Parking Lot at 2:10 AM

blocks.text: Megan is a night-shift nurse. Her boyfriend Jordan lives across town and works a standard nine-to-five, meaning their schedules barely overlap except on weekends.

They have a simple agreement: every night after her shift, Megan checks in on ANLY with location sharing on as she leaves the hospital, and taps again once she gets home. Jordan usually wakes up to see both check-ins waiting.
At 3:00 AM that morning, Jordan woke up and checked his phone out of habit. The first check-in was there—2:10 AM, Hospital Parking Lot. The second one wasn't. Her drive home only took twenty minutes.
He called, and it went straight to voicemail. He tried again—still no answer.

Jordan drove to the hospital and followed her usual route home from there. Ten minutes in, he spotted her car pulled onto the shoulder. Megan was sitting on the curb with a scraped arm and a sprained ankle; another driver had swerved into her lane, forcing her off the road and shattering her phone in the crash.
"I knew someone would come eventually," she said. "I just never expected it to be him—or that fast."
Without that first check-in, Jordan wouldn't have known where to start looking.

articles.title: More Than 1 in 4 Americans Over 65 Live Alone

blocks.text: According to the 2023 Profile of Older Americans published in 2024 by the U.S. Administration for Community Living (ACL), roughly 28% of community-dwelling adults aged 65 and older live alone.
In other words, more than one in four seniors wakes up every morning with nobody else in the house.

Living alone doesn't automatically mean feeling lonely—many older adults cherish their independence and thrive on their own. Yet when you live solo, if you take a fall, feel unwell, or stay indoors for days, there may not be anyone around to notice right away.

A single daily check-in doesn't interfere with an independent lifestyle; it simply lets faraway family know everything is okay each day. And if a check-in ever goes missing, someone will make that first phone call.
Source: U.S. Administration for Community Living, 2023 Profile of Older Americans (2024)

articles.title: She Told Her Carers Which Dive Shop She Was Going Out With

blocks.text: Chloe, a freelance illustrator, went on a solo diving trip to a small island in the Bahamas. Before she left, she did two things: she set her ANLY check-in frequency to every 12 hours, and she posted her itinerary in her ANLY Room, including the name of the dive shop and where she was staying.
On the third day, while walking back from the boat, she slipped on the rocky pier. Her ankle swelled up immediately, and the phone in her shorts pocket fell straight into the ocean.
The dive shop staff took her to the island's only clinic. Without her phone, she couldn't contact anyone, and she couldn't recite a single phone number from memory.

That evening, she missed her check-in. Her best friend Maya in New York saw the alert, checked the itinerary in the Room, and called the dive shop directly. The staff told her exactly where Chloe was.
Maya then called the clinic, finally getting to speak with Chloe. From the US, Maya helped her handle the travel insurance claims and rebooked her ferry back to Nassau.
"I was stuck on an island with no phone," Chloe said, "but someone back home knew exactly who to call."
Sharing your itinerary before a trip takes just two minutes, but when something goes wrong, it can save you hours.

articles.title: She Had an Allergic Reaction at a Kyoto Restaurant, and Her Phone Was at the Hostel

blocks.text: Rachel went on a five-day solo trip to Kyoto. Before leaving, she sent the name of her hostel to her best friend Megan in Chicago, and they agreed that Rachel would check in on ANLY every night when she got back to her room. They usually only caught up every week or two.

On her third night, she went out for dinner, taking only her wallet and leaving her phone at the hostel to charge. The dish she ordered contained shrimp paste, which she was allergic to. After just a few bites, she started having trouble breathing. The restaurant staff called an ambulance and rushed her to the hospital.

That night, she missed her check-in. Megan received the alert, and when her texts went unanswered, she remembered the name of the hostel and gave them a call. The front desk said Rachel had gone out for the evening and hadn't returned yet, but they promised to help call nearby hospitals.

An hour later, the receptionist called Megan back: Rachel was at the hospital and her condition had stabilized. Megan was able to speak with Rachel through the hospital's phone and then helped notify her family back in the US.
"I just went out to grab a quick dinner," Rachel said. "I never expected that one meal would completely cut me off from everyone for the entire night."
When traveling alone, share your accommodation details with a friend. If you miss a check-in, they'll know exactly where to start looking.

articles.title: Eating Alone Can Still Mean Eating Well

blocks.text: Many people assume that living alone means being lonely. But that's not really true.

When you live alone, you get to decide what to have for dinner, what time to go to bed, and whether or not you want to go out on the weekend. You can decorate your space exactly the way you like it, or you can do absolutely nothing and just lie on the couch listening to music all afternoon.
Living solo doesn't require sympathy, and it doesn't need to be explained.
However, this freedom does come with one small trade-off: when you actually need help, there might not be anyone around who knows.

That's why we don't need to change the way we live alone; we just need a very light connection. A simple tap every day lets the people who care about you know that you're doing fine today. The rest of the time, you're still you, completely free and independent.
Eating alone can still mean eating well. Just remember that somewhere far away, someone will see your water drop turn blue.

articles.title: If Something Happens to Me, Who Will Take Care of My Cat?

blocks.text: Olivia lives alone with her cat, Mochi. Once, when she was unexpectedly hospitalized for three days, a sudden thought hit her: If no one knew she was in the hospital, what would happen to Mochi?
For many people who live alone, they aren't actually the only ones in the house. There's also a cat, a dog, or a tank of fish, waiting for them to come home every day.

After that experience, Olivia did three things. She gave a spare key to her friend Kevin, who lives nearby, and added him as a Carer on ANLY. She stuck a note on her fridge detailing Mochi's food portions and the vet's phone number. She also made an agreement with Kevin: if she ever missed a check-in and couldn't be reached, he would go over and check on her.
"I'm not just building a safety net for myself," Olivia said. "I'm doing it for Mochi, too."
Taking good care of yourself is also taking care of the little lives that depend on you.

articles.title: Nearly 1 in 3 U.S. Households Is Just One Person

blocks.text: 1 in 3

According to the Families and Living Arrangements estimates released by the U.S. Census Bureau in November 2026, there are 40.5 million one-person households in the United States. That makes up 30% of all households, meaning nearly 1 in 3 homes has just one person living in it. To put that in perspective, back in 1976, that number was only 21%.
In other words, living alone is no longer a rare choice—it is the new normal of our time. You likely have friends, coworkers, or even parents who are living by themselves right now.

The issue has never been whether living alone is good or bad. The real question is: if something happens, would anyone notice? A daily check-in simply lets the people who care about you know you're okay, every day.
Source: U.S. Census Bureau, Families and Living Arrangements (2026)

articles.title: After Thirty, You Don't Lose Friends; They Just Get Quieter

blocks.text: In your twenties, you see your friends every week, and your group chats are flooded with hundreds of messages a day.
After thirty, someone gets married, someone moves to another city, and someone takes on a demanding new job. The group chats grow quieter, and getting together requires planning a month in advance.

Many people think this means the friendships are fading. But that's not necessarily true. Everyone is just busy navigating their own lives, unsure of how to say "I'm still here" without being intrusive.

One group of friends found a solution: they added each other as Carers on ANLY and check in individually every day. There's no need to make small talk; just seeing each other's water drops turn blue is enough to know everyone is doing well.
If someone checks in late for a few days in a row, someone else will simply ask, "Everything okay lately?" And just like that, they end up scheduling a dinner they haven't had in a long time.
You don't have fewer friends. You just need a quieter way to stay in each other's lives.

articles.title: Three Siblings Teaming Up to Care for Their Parents Back Home

blocks.text: The three siblings had all moved away from their hometown in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. David, the oldest brother, lived in Chicago; Anna, the middle sister, was in Indianapolis; and Emma, the youngest, was in Minneapolis. Their parents lived alone back home. They were still in relatively good health, but they were getting older.

In the past, the siblings would often ask in their group chat, "Who called Mom and Dad recently?" The result was usually either all three calling on the exact same day, or an entire week going by with no one calling at all.

Eventually, they reorganized their approach. Emma helped their parents set up ANLY and added all three siblings as Carers. Now, their parents check in every morning after their walk, and all three kids can see it.

They also made a plan: if their parents miss a check-in, David, who lives the closest, calls first. If he can't reach them, he calls their uncle Bill, who lives next door. Anna is in charge of the Sunday video calls, and Emma handles the monthly doctor appointment reminders.
"We all used to worry a lot, but no one really knew what to do," Anna said. "Now, everyone knows exactly what their role is."
Caring for your parents doesn't mean you have to live with them. With clear roles, the distance doesn't feel so far anymore.

articles.title: Living Alone? 5 Rules for Who Should Get Your Spare Key

blocks.text: Give it to someone who lives close by, ideally someone who can get to your place within twenty minutes.
Choose someone you truly trust, and who is willing to answer their phone in the middle of the night.
Prepare at least two copies: one for a friend or family member, and one for your building manager or landlord.
Add the person holding your key as a Carer on ANLY, so they know to check on you if you miss a check-in.
Remember to ask for the key back if you change your locks or move out.
A spare key is often the deciding factor in whether someone can reach you in time.

articles.title: Every Day, About 113 Older Americans Die After a Fall

blocks.text: 113 a day

According to the CDC's National Center for Health Statistics, about 41,400 adults aged 65 and older died from unintentional falls in the United States in 2023. That is an average of about 113 people every single day. Falls remain the leading cause of injury-related death for older Americans. Looking globally, the World Health Organization estimates that 684,000 people die from falls each year, with older adults at the highest risk.

A fall sounds like a common, everyday accident, but it usually happens when we are least prepared: in the bathroom, on the stairs, or just walking across the living room floor. Often, the real danger is not the fall itself, but the fact that no one knows it happened.
Checking in once a day cannot prevent accidents, but it can shorten that dangerous blank space between falling and being found.
Sources: CDC NCHS Data Brief No. 532; CDC Older Adult Falls Data; WHO Falls Fact Sheet

articles.title: Her Husband Was Relocated to Vietnam, and She Caught a High Fever Alone with the Baby

blocks.text: Hannah's husband was relocated to Vietnam for work, only flying back to the U.S. three or four times a year. She lived in Seattle with their one-year-old son, while her parents were down in Portland. The couple usually stayed in touch through text messages, but her husband was often busy and replied late.
Before he left, they set up ANLY together. Hannah checked in every morning before 9:00 AM. Her husband, her mom, and her close friend Kate, who lived in the same neighborhood, were all her Carers.
That Saturday, Hannah caught a terrible fever that spiked near 104 degrees. Exhausted, she fell asleep on the couch holding her baby. By noon, her check-in still had not appeared.

Kate received the alert. When Hannah didn't pick up her phone, Kate walked straight over and rang the doorbell. Hannah barely managed to get up and open the door. Seeing how sick she was, Kate immediately took the baby and then drove Hannah to the ER.
When her husband saw the messages in Vietnam, he immediately called Kate to thank her and booked a flight back to Seattle that very night.
"My husband is seven thousand miles away," Hannah said. "But Kate is only a few blocks down the street."
In an expat family, the partner who stays behind needs a safety net that is a little closer to home.

articles.title: 3 Small Things You Can Do on a Bad Day

blocks.text: Get something to eat or drink. When you're feeling down, your body is often more exhausted than you realize.
Send a quick message to someone you trust. You don't need to explain much—just saying "I'm a bit drained today" is enough.
Check in a little early. It's not about reassuring someone else, but reminding yourself: today, you still need to take good care of yourself.
On a bad day, you don't have to bounce back right away. But you can start by doing one small, kind thing for yourself.

articles.title: How to Pick a Check-In Moment You Won't Forget

blocks.text: Tie it to something you already do every day, like having your first cup of coffee, finishing your commute, or brushing your teeth at night.
Pick a moment when you're almost always awake with your phone nearby. If you sleep in on weekends, don't pick the moment you first wake up.
If your daily schedule changes a lot, pick a later moment in the day so you won't feel rushed.
The best check-in moment is the one that naturally becomes a habit.

articles.title: After Retirement, Checking In Became Dad's Reason to Go Out

blocks.text: Mr. Davis retired this past June. After thirty years of leaving for work at 7:00 AM every day, he suddenly didn't know what to do with his mornings.
His son lives in Seattle and his daughter is in Los Angeles. Both noticed their dad was getting quieter on the phone. Their mom mentioned he was spending most days just sitting at home watching TV.

His daughter came up with an idea. She helped him set up ANLY and asked him to take a walk in the nearby park every morning, then check in when he was done. "That way, we'll know you got out of the house today."

At first, he thought it was a bit unnecessary, but he's a man of his word. Every morning, he headed out right on schedule. Slowly, he got to know a morning walking group at the park, and later he even joined a community woodworking class.
Lately, his check-ins have been getting later and later. When his daughter asked him why, he replied, "I check in after my woodworking class now. Is that a problem?"
Retirement isn't just about leaving a job; it's about finding a new rhythm in life. Sometimes, a small daily promise is all it takes to take that first step.

articles.title: When the Hurricane Flooded the House, Grandma Climbed to the Second Floor

blocks.text: Grandma lives alone in a two-story house near the Louisiana coast. Her grandson, Jake, works in Chicago and visits her about once a month. He helped her set up ANLY, and they made a habit of her checking in every morning after she finished watering her plants.

That year, a hurricane brought massive flooding. In the middle of the night, water started pouring into the first floor. Grandma is older but very calm; she grabbed a flashlight and climbed up to the second floor. Her phone was left charging in the living room downstairs, and she couldn't go back for it.
That morning, her check-in never came. Later, Jake got an alert. He tried calling her, but no one answered. Then he saw on the news that her town was severely flooded.

He immediately called the local sheriff's office. They told him the water was above knee-level in many neighborhoods and they were going door-to-door checking on elderly residents. Jake gave them Grandma's address. First responders took a rescue boat over and found her on the second floor. She was cold and hungry, but safe.
"I was in Chicago and couldn't do anything myself," Jake said. "But at least I knew exactly who to call right away."
During a natural disaster, what seniors living alone need most is for someone to notice something is wrong earlier than usual.

articles.title: What Happens If You Forget to Check In?

blocks.text: Many people ask when they first use ANLY: What if I just forget to check in? Will everyone panic?
You can pick a time of day that works for you and make it a habit to check in.
If your check-in time runs out, your Carers get an alert.
The first thing people usually do when they get an alert is text or call you; most of the time, you're just busy.
If you know you'll be late checking in, like when you're on a flight or in a meeting, you can let your Carers know ahead of time.
Once you catch up and check in, Wally turns blue, and everyone knows you're safe.
Missing a check-in doesn't mean something bad happened. It just lets the people who care about you know it's time to check in on you.

articles.title: 5 Simple Steps to Help Your Parents Set Up ANLY

blocks.text: Help them pick a time of day to check in and make it a habit, like after their morning walk or breakfast.
Make the font size larger on their phone and put the ANLY app on the home screen where it's easy to find.
Decide together who their Carers should be: siblings, nearby relatives, or neighbors.
Ask if they want to turn on location sharing for their check-ins, and let them make the decision.
Practice checking in with them once a day for the first week until it becomes a habit.
Technology isn't the hard part. The hard part is helping your parents feel like this is about peace of mind for everyone, not about keeping tabs on them.

articles.title: Three Days Without Cell Service, but Everyone Knew the Plan

blocks.text: Aaron shoots documentary films about mountaineering. Before heading into remote areas, he always does the same thing: he posts his itinerary in his ANLY Room, noting the dates he will be without cell service and the name of his local guide. He also keeps his location sharing on for the entire trip.

While trekking in northern Pakistan, he expected to have no signal for almost three days. On the morning he started the trail, he checked in at the trailhead and set his ANLY check-in frequency to every 3 days, planning to check in again when he reached a village at the end of the route on the third evening.

The third evening passed, and he did not check in. By the fourth day, his producer Ivy and his other Carers received a missed check-in alert. Ivy opened the Room, and the plan was right there: the route, the dates, the guide's name, and the guide company's phone number.

Ivy called the company, and they reached the guide via satellite phone. It turned out a landslide had blocked the trail, forcing the group to take a longer detour. Aaron had twisted his knee during the detour and was moving slowly, but the guide stayed right by his side. The company dispatched a jeep to pick them up at the next village.
"If that plan wasn't in the Room, Ivy wouldn't have known who to call," Aaron said. "She would have just been waiting."
Before heading into an area with no cell service, tell your Carers: where you are going, when, and who you are with.

articles.title: 5 Things to Remember Before a Solo Road Trip

blocks.text: Tell a friend your route and estimated time of arrival before you hit the road.
Take a break every two hours and check in at the rest stop, and turn on location sharing for your check-ins if you need it.
Check ahead of time to see where you might lose cell service along the way.
Keep water, a portable charger, a flashlight, and a warm jacket in your car.
Check in as soon as you arrive, so the people waiting for you know you made it.
Driving alone gives you a lot of freedom, but you still want someone to know roughly where you are.

articles.title: 7 Things to Do Before Traveling Solo to a Remote Country

blocks.text: Book a local guide in remote areas and save both their personal and company phone numbers.
Enroll your trip in the Smart Traveler Enrollment Program (STEP).
Post your itinerary and dates in your ANLY Room, making sure to note any days you expect to be without a signal.
Adjust your check-in frequency based on your plans, such as every 12 hours.
Decide when to turn on location sharing for your check-ins, like before a hike, a border crossing, or a long drive.
Bring a power bank and a backup way to communicate, like a local SIM card or a satellite messenger.
Agree with your Carers on what to do if you miss a check-in—who they should call and how long they should wait.
Adventure is a lot more fun when you know someone has your back.

articles.title: 5 Things to Tell Your Carers Before a Hike

blocks.text: Which route you're taking and which trailhead you're starting from.
What time you plan to be back down, and when they should start reaching out if they haven't heard from you.
Who you're going with, and the phone number of a hiking buddy.
If you're driving, send your license plate and where you parked to a friend.
Check in at the trailhead, at the summit, and when you're back down, and turn on location sharing for your check-ins if you need it.
These details only take five minutes to share, but if something goes wrong, they can save search and rescue teams hours of time.
